Messages.Body:
I'm really quite amazed at the amount of bitching about things that
DON'T win in big tournaments, and the complete dearth of bitching about
things that DO win in big tournaments.

I was just reading about Gehenna events--apparently people think
they're devastating if not ganged up on. There is usually a lot of
fuss about Protect Thine Own. And LSJ himself made some comment about
weenie Auspex being strong, although I can't remember where I saw it.

And yet, none of these decks are even close to being dominant in the
tournament scene. Since Gehenna was printed, there haven't been many
(any?) qualifier- or continental championship-level tournament winning
Gehenna decks. In major continental championships, I only know of one
PTO called in any of the four finals games in the last two years, and
only one weenie Auspex deck among the 20 decks involved.

In the last two years, the finalist decks at the North American and
European championships (a combined 20 decks) breaks down as follows:

2004 NAC
!Malk bleed
!Toreador embrace
Ventrue (OBF)
CEL guns
Ventrue (OBF)
2004 EC
Ventrue (OBF)
Malkavian vote
!Malk bleed
War Ghouls
Lucas Halton wall
2005 NAC
Ventrue (OBF)
Ventrue (no OBF)
Nos princes
Giovanni
CEL guns
2005 EC
Panders
Ventrue (OBF)
!Malk bleed
Ventrue (OBF)
Giovanni

By category:
5 stealth bleeders
9 obf voters
1 non-obf voter
2 rush combat
1 weenie embrace
1 War Ghoul
1 Intercept wall

So, weenie intercept was not dominant in any way. "Gehenna event
decks" weren't represented at all--I played in all of these four
tournaments and didn't even encounter any in the preliminary rounds.
Stealth vote, on the other hand, is grossly overrepresented, perhaps
under-complained-about.

Why no bitching about stealth vote? Forgotten Labyrinth is hugely
good, and there's no intercept card that matches it. Granted, people
bitch about Arika from time to time, but I think most of the Ventrue
with OBF decks would work fine with Marcus Vitel + Queen Anne +
Lucinde.

It seems like a lot of what people bitch about is actually stuff that
wins or is omnipresent in the last-chance qualifier (incidentally).
Going back to the last-chance qualifier finalists in the last two
years, much more weenie AUS and embrace hordes existed:

2005 NAC LCQ
Black Hand
?
2005 EC LCQ
Ravnos embrace
Ravnos embrace
?
2006 NAC LCQ
something Ventrue
Ravnos embrace
Huitzilopochtli + Great Beast
?
2006 EC LCQ
2 Auspex intercept wall
?

Now, I don't have all of the data (maybe someone could help fill this
out?), but I wouldn't be surprised if there were at least one
additional intercept deck and one additional embrace deck, some
stealth-bleed and some stealth-vote, and absolutely no Gehenna event
decks at all.

I suppose I'm making this post for three reasons:
1) I want to know what was played at the last 4 last-chance qualifiers
2) I want to know why everyone's so mad about decks which aren't so
great
3) I want to know whether something should be done about the decks
which are actually dominant

And I suppose the last two answers are probably
2) Cause they are dominant, in that playgroup
3) no

I know if I were in charge, Week of Nightmares and Palla Grande would
only give +1 bleed to vampires of that clan with capacity >2, just to
get all masters that generate +20 bleed back down to something
reasonable. But after writing this, I have to wonder whether that's
only a minor problem, and therefore not worth changing, given the
actual spread of deck types at the highest level of tournament play.

So in conclusion:
--Hey, anybody know what was played in the qualifiers?
--To the complainers, Gehenna events / PTO / AUS wall etc. isn't so
bad, you just have a jerkass in your playgroup who likes to ruin the
game and he's not anything to be worried about at any higher-level
tournament,
-- Current decktypes have a good amount of diversity, except a bit top
heavy with stealth-vote, but there's no immediate need to fix that.

-- Brian

Messages.Body:
firstco...@aol.com wrote:
> I suppose I'm making this post for three reasons:
> 1) I want to know what was played at the last 4 last-chance qualifiers
> 2) I want to know why everyone's so mad about decks which aren't so

'Cause the cards you mention (Gehenna Events and PTO) are problematic,
primarily, for reasons other than winning the game. Both Gehenna Events
and PTO 'cause problems by wildly disrupting the game (Gehenna Events
always, and PTO when it is used in the way that tends to make most
folks mad--i.e. cross table) in the sense that people play them and
they don't win--they just make someone else win, usually randomly.
Which is, for my money, that which people (well, the competetive minded
ones) really object to. No one is bothered by decks that win by being
effective. People are bothered by decks that turn the game into a
random crap shoot.

Gehenna Event decks are incredibly damaging to the table. Sometimes the
deck that plays the Events can take advanatge enough to win, but more
often than not, they don't. They just make the table a crazy mess, slow
everything down in a irritating way ("What happens when I have the
audacity to play this card in conjunction with those 5 cards on the
other side of the table with lots of text on them?"). PTO often gets
called cross table in some crazy attempt to "balance the table", which
generally leads to outrage. And someone random (i.e. not the PTO guy)
winning. Which people don't like. Anarch Revolt, pre repair, did the
same thing. So it got repaired.

The problem is rarely "this deck wins too much". It is "this deck
demolishes the table, and yet doesn't win enough."

> 3) I want to know whether something should be done about the decks

> which are actually dominant.

Unlikely. 'Cause the deck types that are dominant (S+B, stealth vote,
whatever) win without demolishing the table. They sit down, oust their
prey, and win. Which is what people like to see in a game. And these
sorts of things are usually controlled by self correcting measures--the
defenses of good decks are worth playing in a general sense, so they
show up (i.e. bleed bounce and vote defense). It is possible that every
once and a while, a card/strategy shows up and is *too* effective, but
those aren't common, and tend to get fixed eventually.

-Peter

If you're looking for a polite, well-reasoned response from people it's
generally advised not to paint a wide range of possibly related
activities and people with the same brush. Using the word "bitching"
implies that people are complaining without any good reason, and
without backing up their arguments, so of course that's a negative
thing. If this were universally the case, you'd be right to criticize
this kind of behavior. However, it's my impression that a fair number
of players have given some fairly well thought out arguments for why
they think certain things are bad for the game. You don't have to
agree with these arguments, but when you make a blanket
characterization of them as "bitching" you're essentially precluding
the possibility of reasoned discussion. Some people do bitch and moan,
and my feeling is that they should generally just be ignored. Others
have reasonable arguments, and those are the ones that deserve
attention (though ironically people often pay the most attention to the
least attention-worthy posters).

Starting a conversation with this kind of rhetoric would be liking me
asking you: "why are you such an asshole?" I might pretend that I'm
asking a serious question to which I expect a serious response, but my
choice of words has already betrayed a general unwillingness to discuss
anything. When you start this topic by asking others "why are you
bitching?", you assume/imply that they are just bitching. So try to be
a little more polite.

> And yet, none of these decks are even close to being dominant in the
> tournament scene. Since Gehenna was printed, there haven't been many

> Gehenna decks. In major continental championships, I only know of one

I don't know what universe you live in, but in the one I've been
inhabiting weenie auspex (or midcap mono-AUS) is a very strong
archetype. The primary reasons for the success of such a strategy, in
my analysis, is the over-reliance on high-stealth, heavy-payload style
decks at many tournaments. A metagame more geared towards combat is
not especially friendly for the auspex wall decks.

> In the last two years, the finalist decks at the North American and
> European championships (a combined 20 decks) breaks down as follows:

You might think these statistics are meaningful, but I really don't.
You're looking at only 20 decks out of all the players at these events
(some of which were quite large, and which in and of themselves hardly
represent the entire range of competetive VTES), and assuming that they
are a representative sample of what works. In large tournaments full
off good players and good decks, luck is very important. If seating
orders or deck shuffles had been different throughout the day the
results could have been very different.

And again, as Peter says, the problem isn't decks that win. The
problem is decks that break the table in an obnoxious way whether or
not they win.

> Why no bitching about stealth vote? Forgotten Labyrinth is hugely
> good, and there's no intercept card that matches it. Granted, people
> bitch about Arika from time to time, but I think most of the Ventrue

You're certainly right that Ventrue with obfuscate would be good even

No deck can guarantee that your predator won't oust you. Most wall
decks do a very good job of defening agaisnt stealth+x style strategies
by packing tons of intercept, bounce, and vote defense. However, a
good combat deck should crush a wall deck prey without any trouble at
all. It is possible for the wall player to pack more combat defense,
but then he'll be less able to reliably shut down bleed and vote decks.
Plus, he'll probably end up with a more expensive crypt since he'll
need to run two ore more disciplines instead of just one
(disciplineless combat defense is not sufficient against a dedicated
rush deck--except maybe weenie pot).

Another option available for the predator of a wall deck is to make a
deal with his grandprey. Help your grandprey munch his way through his
first two VPs (your own forward motion is probably halted anyhow, so
send your offense elsewhere), then team up to kill the wall in the 3
player phase and withdraw. You give away your chance of winning, but
you're claiming that you never had one anyhow. 2 vp is better than 0.

have the word "Gehenna" written on them. If examples of getting
screwed by Gehenna were as clean-cut as the one you present, the
problem would be largely non-existent. But they aren't, and even your
example fails to make a decent analogy. First, Ventrue HQ requires a
specific clan to play it. Fall of the Camarilla does not. Second,
Ventrue HQ can be dealt with by a wide variety of fairly flexible
means, from SRing it immediately to burning it or stealing it later (it
is a location after all). In some cases, one could even contest it.
Further, the effect is totally different. In both fictional examples,
you do happen to be gaining an advantage by shutting down your
predator's ability to pass votes against you. In one case, you can
stop one vote a turn. In the other, you stop all of them. One card
will prevent your predator from playing a potentially very large
portion of their deck (traditions, parity shift, etc.). The other
won't. And what if the other vote deck at the table isn't even your
predator or prey? One of these cards gives you a resource that you can
you use to your own advantage, and to help/hurt other players according
to the needs of your position. The other just screws someone else.
It's pretty obvious that these are different things.

Firstly, "bitching" isn't always negative. For example, in the above,
I state my amazement that there isn't MORE bitching about a thing.

for more of it.

If you took the first part to be insulting, then I apologize, because
that's not how I meant it. The second part, however, bemoans a lack of
bitching about other things, implying that bitching can be useful.
Taken together, the opening paragraph was not supposed to paint all
comments against [x] as baseless, nor people concerned about [x] as
moronic, but rather all comments against [x] as not as important as
comments against [y] would be, which are conspicuously missing.

playtesting. By the end, though, we were all convinced through play
that they weren't nearly as abusable as we had originally thought, and
that the ones that were abusive or disruptive had been sufficiently
reworded as to be acceptable. The sheer volume of people who, through
years of play, have failed to come to this conclusion leaves me
wondering, "Why is this still a big deal, when there are so many other
things that need concern?" It's like having more meth labs in your
county than anywhere else in America, and yet people want an increase
in traffic cops.

> > reasonable.
>

What is this, an invitation to a fight? Stop missing the point. The
first post wasn't made to start a flame war, it was made to understand
why, of two or more things, only those which are less powerful are
causing concern. This made itself apparent to at least some of the
other readers, judging from their responses.

> > actual spread of deck types at the highest level of tournament play.
>
> Oh wait. You're making an argument. It's a good thing I can tell the
> difference, even if you can't.

I'm going to ignore this and continue to reply to your post, because
other than this insult, your post contains interesting points which
deserve responding to.

be a series of statements which support a conclusion, whereas the above
is more of a rhetorical question or a musing. Either way, I fail to
see how some good old-fashioned bitching is unable to form a very
important part of an argument. In fact, I'd say the bitching on THIS
VERY NEWSGROUP was likely influential in the changing of cards for
years now, in dozens of cases.

In conclusion, there's bitching about something you don't understand,
without fundament. There's bitching about something in the proper
forum (possibly this one) in order to discern other people's opinions
on the subject. And then there's looking at all the facts and going,

presented to another with the facts, likely going to cause another
"yeah, that IS kind of messed up" response, which is how broke cards

problem comes up again--people fear seeing a lot of heavy Gehenna Event

> events more disruptive?

likely to show up.

aren't any better at winning than Gehenna+Kindred decks, then, well,
they'll infect the environment for a bit while they are still new, make
everyone mad, not win much, and again get weeded out of the gene pool.

winning than Gehenna+Kindred decks, they'll see play a lot. Which is

decks that don't win but screw up the game for everyone), they still
will tend to make the game suck for eveyone else ("Uhh, lets see. I
can't replace my cards, my cards cost an extra blood, I can't hunt, I
have to hunt, the Camarilla don't exist, all of my actions effectively
have -1 stealth, hunting has effectively -2 stealth, which I can't do

> get votes off. Lasombra decks work pretty good in that respect
> but most of the other sorts of classic vote decks don't have a
> lot of ready sources of stealth

Ventrue, in their original (G1)ory, aren't what they used to be. But
Lasombra, Nosferatu, Malkavian, Gangrel, some Tzimisce, and _most
notably_ G2+G3 Ventrue all have access to plenty of stealth and make
excellent vote decks. Also please note that most of them have a S:CE
card that fits their disciplines.

> I guess if you find vote decks to be consistent then I respect
> your opinion about it. But I've just never observed that myself.

Maybe you build and play vote decks differently than I do. I am best
at intercept or bruise and bleed; stealth vote is all the way on the
other side of the color wheel for me. I decided to play it 2 or 3
years ago because I am poorest at it, and in that time I have learned
these three rules for building and playing vote decks:

1.) You don't need vote lock to pass a vote. If you play KRC, and
then call terms 3 / 1 without discussing it, players will usually take
the one on their prey as a gesture of goodwill and vote for it. (This
rule is out the window when your prey is in ousting range.)

2.) You DO need vote lock to completely devastate a table. Weenie
voters need to have lock, cause everyone will certainly cast all of
their votes against anything they call.

3.) Your crypt should be only titled vampires. If you need more
weenies to call votes, play with 3rd Tradition or Creation Rites or
whatever.

> > (do you know how easily Forgotten Labyrinth + Private Audience
> > passes almost any vote?)
>
> Actually, I'm not taking such a thing into account, no. I mean,
> Private Audience - besides being kind of random in its effect -
> is like Bewitching Oration and Awe: if you have to rely on them,
> they tend to slow your deck down when don't draw them. And

True, so don't rely on them. Use votes that help pass themselves, like
KRC.

> even having to put them into your deck robs it of other moving
> parts, like stealth or voter caps. If it pops up and allows
> you to pass a key vote at a critcical moment and that's what
> makes the game (like your Pander deck getting its LoP passed),
> then fine. But that strikes me as an unusual property of a
> "consistent" deck. Usually, I would think making a vote deck
> work consistently would hinge on knowing you can pass lots of
> votes consistently.

"Passing lots of votes consistently" is like "bleeding every turn
consistently": It requires lots of cards, and scares the table
sometimes. Voting sporadically, and using Bewitching (or Awe, etc.) as
a finisher is rather like bleeding for 1 or 2 sporadically, and using
Conditioning as a finisher.

> You always want to look inoffensive, I agree - just not at the cost
> of actually _being_ inoffensive. If you have vote lock, then you
> _will_ look offensive. If you don't, the problem is that you
> have dance real fast to get around it. And it's difficult to do
> that dance to get an oust.

If you spend the first 7 turns voting here and there, and setting up
your hand in the meanwhile, then on turn 8 or 9 you can probably do the
dance once or (if you're lucky) twice, which would net you 1 or (if
you're lucky) 2 VPs.

> > Or more concisely put, vote decks, by using large minions, have most of
> > their power hidden effectively in their hand.
>
> I think that's where our perceptions diverge. If Arika's on the
> table, I just assume the power is in the hand. I don't care
> if I haven't seen the actual cards and I don't think most others
> do, either.

I think people feel confident that Arika has power in her hand, sure.
I was only saying that if there's also power on the table, then I think
it's more threatening, because it's a REAL threat instead of a
projected one. 20 !Toreadors would almost always scare me more than
Arika, even with TWO other Ventrue. If my cross table ally asks for
help with Arika, then I might help, I might not. You don't have to ask
for help against 20 !Toreadors cause the table is already scared and is
doing what it can.

-- Brian

> See, that is not actually the case. Maybe it is just your play
> environment, but I rarely see cross table activity do anything other
> than make someone else win.

Peter, we agree in many things, but all the difference between our
arguments in the end is from a different view of VTES as a multiplayer
game.

IMO good play in VTES (and i am still not able to handle this level of
play) is the ability to read the whole table, interfere at the whole
table in your own interest and especially defend against your predator.
Playing against your left gives you VPs, playing against your right let
your survive. The best player will interfere at the whole table with
the fewest ressources as possible, so you often dont notice that they
interfere. Thats another reason why vote decks are strong, you can for
example help another vote without using any cards or tapping any
minions just by giving your votes. Because bad crosstable activities
make more noise (like rushing your grandprey) doenst mean that the
silent good crosstable activities arent important and not be very
effective in winning the game.

> They are more often won by ousting your prey. I fail to see how deals
> make you win, as any deal that is going to make you win is a deal that
> your opponents should not be making. So why are they making them?

A standard situation. 4 player table A, B, C, D. Lets say D is the
strongest deck at the monent, he will kill A probably in five rounds
(he can play a S&B deck, a Rush deck - not important). Because A will
be weakened in a few turns, he will not make pressure on B, so C is
also in trouble. If A and C are S&B decks that can only go against
their prey, they will lose. If A is a vote deck, it can make a simple
deal with C. "We both kill our preys and afterwards we fight for the
GW. We start with D." With that deal and the crosstable ability of A
(to oust its predator) they are able to kill D before he can kill A. B
if he has no crosstable ability will not be able to stop that
happening, because his pressure on C will not be fast enough. (Please
dont be nitpicking - i know sometimes A and C are already toasted, than
there is nothing that can save them.)

Frank

someone who you think is doing to well or "balancing the table" to be a
pointless endeavor, as most of the time, it doesn't actually work the
